clue.text: Ring up the world? Quite the opposite

definitions.text: Ring up the world? Quite the opposite

parts.words: Ring up the world? Quite the opposite
parts.note: a line of latitude is a ring round the globe; this one is not up at the top but down near the South Pole

explanation.surface: Someone thinks of telephoning the whole planet, then decides the opposite is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring up' tempts you to think of telephoning. Read it as a ring at the top of the world, and 'the opposite' moves it to the bottom: a ring down at the southern end.
explanation.definitionFit: The southern polar parallel is a ring around the bottom of the globe, the opposite of its northern counterpart.

clue.text: Fairly drab Friday food? Bring in the meat!

indicators.note: the cut of beef is brought into the Friday dish, placed inside it

parts.note: fish is traditionally eaten on Fridays by Catholics abstaining from meat
rump is a cut of beef

explanation.surface: A cook switches from the dull Friday fish dish and calls for the meat course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bring in' signals the container. Fish on Friday is the old Catholic custom of avoiding meat that day; 'Fairly' is part of the definition, not a filler.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone frumpish dresses dowdily and unfashionably, which is to say rather drab.

clue.text: Bad men undermining work after revolution

indicators.note: in a down clue the soldiers sit underneath the work, below it in the grid
the word for work is turned round, so it reads backwards

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work
OR, other ranks, is the usual crossword abbreviation for soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Workers sabotage a job following a political uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after revolution' reverses the opus; 'undermining' works because in a down entry the soldiers sit beneath it.
explanation.definitionFit: Poor work is bad work: the two adjectives are synonyms for low quality.

clue.text: Russian fighter fell down almost, due to medical condition

parts.note: the MiG is a Russian fighter aircraft

indicators.note: the last letter of the verb is left off, so it is not quite complete

parts.note: rain fell down, so it rained

explanation.surface: A Russian jet crashes, and the cause is put down to the pilot's illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims RAINED to RAINE, from 'fell down' read as rain falling.
explanation.definitionFit: A severe recurring headache, often with nausea, is a recognised medical condition.

clue.text: The man leading Earth's revolution is a god

indicators.note: the man comes first, in front of the reversed earth

parts.note: a man is referred to as he

indicators.note: the word for earth is turned right round, so it reads backwards

parts.note: earth means soil

explanation.surface: A man spearheading a world revolution is hailed as divine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolution' reverses the earth, and 'leading' puts the man in front; 'Earth' is ground, not the planet.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the sun was personified as a deity who drove his chariot across the sky.

clue.text: Debility in one half of continent followed by the other

indicators.note: the continent's name is cut in two and the front half used

parts.note: Asia is a continent
then means next, followed by
the other half of the continent's name, its back two letters

explanation.surface: Weakness strikes one half of a continent and then spreads to the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one half of' and 'the other' split the continent's name in two, with 'followed by' slotted between the halves.
explanation.definitionFit: This medical term means physical weakness or lack of strength, the same as debility.

clue.text: Dog getting caught, one of a funny pair

parts.note: C is the cricket scoring abbreviation for caught
Ollie, Oliver Hardy, partner of Stan Laurel in the comedy double act

explanation.surface: A dog is captured, belonging to one of a comic duo.
explanation.walkthrough: Laurel and Hardy were known as Stan and Ollie.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheepdog breed from Scotland, widely kept as a working or family dog.

clue.text: Chemical diet — a character's transformed

indicators.note: the letters of the three words are changed in form, rearranged

explanation.surface: A person's character is said to be changed by their diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transformed' rearranges DIET, A and CHARACTERS, the S of the possessive counting as a letter here.
explanation.definitionFit: A sugar built from four simple sugar units is a chemical compound, a carbohydrate.

clue.text: Nasty reactions to drug

indicators.note: the reactions are messed up, made unpleasant, so their letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A warning that a drug causes unpleasant side effects.
explanation.definitionFit: To drug someone with a narcotic, putting them into a stupor, is the verb meaning sedate.

clue.text: Member coming from the centre made a speech?

definitions.meaning: a rod radiating from the hub of a wheel
past tense of talk, said something

explanation.surface: A politician in the middle of the party gives an address.
explanation.definitionFit: One word serves both as a wheel's radiating rod and the past tense of talk.

clue.text: A doctor full of filth — potential abuser of patient?

indicators.note: the doctor's abbreviation is filled with the word for filth

parts.note: mire is mud or filth

explanation.surface: A dirty doctor might be a danger to someone in his care.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: a fan of someone patient, perhaps, or a person whose attentions to a hospital patient are suspect.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone attracted to another person is a fan who might, in the cryptic picture, pester a patient.

clue.text: With this therapeutic device one's home and healthy, right?

parts.note: in means at home
hale means healthy, as in hale and hearty

explanation.surface: With this medical gadget a patient can be at home and well again.
explanation.definitionFit: An asthmatic uses this handheld device to breathe in medicine, so it is a treatment aid.

clue.text: Extract item from box of ornaments?

definitions.meaning: a short excerpt from a film
a hair or jewellery fastener kept with ornaments

explanation.surface: Someone takes a piece out of a box of decorations.
explanation.definitionFit: One word covers both a short film excerpt and a decorative fastener kept in a jewellery box.

clue.text: East Anglian town records nonconformists

parts.note: Diss is a market town in Norfolk, in East Anglia
enters means records, as in a ledger

explanation.surface: A Norfolk town's register lists its religious dissidents.
explanation.walkthrough: DISS is a small market town in Norfolk, in the east of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Protestants who broke from the Church of England were called nonconformists or by this name.

clue.text: Saint — he suffers with fast

indicators.note: the saint and he are put through torment, so their letters are mangled

explanation.surface: A holy man endures hunger while fasting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suffers' rearranges SAINT and HE. 'Fast' looks like going without food, but it means quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something hurriedly means doing it quickly, so the phrase is an adverb for fast.

clue.text: Society girl embraces friend, a noted fellow

indicators.note: the society letter and the girl together hug the friend, holding it between them

parts.note: Ann is a girl's name
a chum is a friend

explanation.surface: A debutante hugs her pal, a well-known man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'noted' is a pun: Robert Schumann was a German composer, a man of notes.
explanation.definitionFit: A German Romantic composer is a man famous for his musical notes, hence noted.

clue.text: Company importing wine is manageable

indicators.note: the company brings the wine inside itself

parts.note: PLC, public limited company
Asti is an Italian sparkling wine

explanation.surface: A firm brings in wine and finds the business easy to run.
explanation.definitionFit: Something malleable can be shaped or controlled easily, hence manageable.

clue.text: See money before crooks

parts.note: pre is a prefix meaning before
crooks are bends or curves

explanation.surface: An instruction to look at the cash ahead of the criminals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is a bishop's diocese, not look; 'crooks' are bends, not criminals.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral's stipend paid to a canon from its revenues is money belonging to a bishop's diocese.

clue.text: Careful nevertheless to hold on to gold

indicators.note: the word for nevertheless keeps the gold within it

parts.note: though means nevertheless
OR is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Be careful, all the same, to keep a grip on the gold.
explanation.definitionFit: A meticulous person who is painstaking is careful in every detail.

clue.text: Paid-up member, which vicar definitely is

definitions.meaning: the phrase vicar definitely holds the letters C, A, R, D within it, so it is a holder of them

explanation.surface: A clergyman is certainly a fully subscribed member of the club.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is cryptic: the letters running across 'viCAR Definitely' spell CARD, so the phrase holds a card.
explanation.definitionFit: A fully paid member carries a membership card, which makes them its holder.

clue.text: Garment of paper set on light removing hem

indicators.note: in a down clue the paper sits on top of the rest

parts.note: rag is slang for a newspaper

indicators.note: in a down clue the hem is the bottom edge, so the last letter of the word goes

parts.note: to light on something is to land or alight

explanation.surface: A piece of clothing made of paper is set alight, losing its edging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'light' is the verb alight, LAND; 'removing hem' drops its bottom letter D in this down entry. 'set on' puts RAG above it.
explanation.definitionFit: A coat or sweater with sleeves running to the collar is named after Lord Raglan; also such a coat.

clue.text: Monkey's laziness — lowest possible score issued

indicators.note: the zero is sent out of the word, so it is removed

parts.note: languor means listlessness or laziness
O, a zero, the lowest score

explanation.surface: A monkey's idleness earns it a mark of nil.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-tailed Asian leaf-eating primate is a kind of monkey.

clue.text: Bear has something to go through backwards

indicators.note: the word for the ring is written from end to start

parts.note: a hoop is a ring that circus animals jump through

explanation.surface: A circus bear has to jump through something going the wrong way.
explanation.definitionFit: Winnie-the-Pooh is A. A. Milne's famous storybook bear.

clue.text: This person in African country brought back government system

indicators.note: the setter goes inside the reversed country
the country's name is returned, read in reverse

parts.note: Niger is a country in West Africa
this person is the setter, me

explanation.surface: The setter, back in an African state, reports on its political system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' reverses the country before 'in' puts the setter inside it; 'This person' is the usual crossword way for the setter to say me.
explanation.definitionFit: A regime or system of rule, or a prescribed course of treatment, is the sense here of a governing scheme.

clue.text: Entrance of old character holding old mother back

indicators.note: the whole assembly is then read in reverse order
the ancient letter keeps the old mother inside it

parts.note: a rune is a letter of an ancient alphabet
ma is mother

explanation.surface: An ancient letter at a doorway encloses an elderly mother, pointing backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' puts OMA inside RUNE, giving RUOMANE; 'back' reverses it all. 'Entrance' is the verb, to charm, not a doorway.
explanation.definitionFit: To charm or captivate someone is to fill them with love, as the verb entrance means.

clue.text: Mob foolish without leader

indicators.note: the word for foolish loses its first letter, its head

parts.note: barmy is British slang for mad or foolish

explanation.surface: A crowd behaving stupidly with nobody in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: BARMY is British slang for crazy or daft.
explanation.definitionFit: A huge crowd can be called a host or mob, as in an army of fans.

clue.text: Get in the head to teach — not standard!

definitions.meaning: to memorise, take knowledge into the mind
in dialect or nonstandard English the word is used to mean teach

explanation.surface: Memorise something so you can instruct others, though the method is unorthodox.
explanation.definitionFit: To acquire knowledge is to take it into the head; dialect also uses the verb for instructing.

clue.text: A foreign mother piled on the years without a blemish

parts.note: un is French for a
a dam is the mother of an animal
to grow older is to have aged

explanation.surface: A foreign mother grew older but kept her skin unmarked.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unharmed is intact and free of marks or flaws, so it has no blemish.
